utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom this is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon, Bronagh McKenna, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't hear any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic I just want to be sure that everybody can hear the English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can everyone hear the English interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Interpreter. We didn't hear you up to now. Anybody else? Judge, can you hear? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I remind once again that you are bound by the oath that you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Gajic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yesterday, page 7, lines 11 through 15 of the LiveNote, you explained that during the war the security administration was particularly concerned about combat operations that took place closer to the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness Exhibit P1926, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just briefly, General, Mr. Lukic discussed this document with you yesterday. This is at pages 14 to 15 of the LiveNote. And as we see, it's a report from the security department of the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina, dated the 1st of July, 1994, and it's submitted to the security administration of the VJ General Staff, as well as to the security department of the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina. And yesterday, Mr. Lukic asked you whether you remembered seeing documents of this kind or indeed receiving documents of this kind during the war, and you responded: "Mr. Lukic, as far as I remember, there may have been several documents like this from the SVK. As for the VRS, we received none at all or none that I can remember." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir. If I may just add one thing. What I had in mind was the formal procedure [as interpreted] for documents under the rules and documents and records of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Can we -- Mr. Saxon has asked for a moment. Maybe if you can just wait for him. Are you okay now, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, page 3, line 10. He said the formal appearance of the document or the format of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a correction, not an objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right, General. I want to make sure that I understand your testimony, and we've just had a correction from -- from Mr. Lukic. So what you wanted to add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What he wanted to say is instead of "formal procedure," "formal appearance" of the documents. In other words, the format of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So -- so -- very well. In other words, you don't recall -- as far as you remember, you did not receive documents in this format from the VRS.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir. That's precisely what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you, if we can, P2179, please. General, this document, it's dated the 14th of May, 1995. It's from the intelligence and security sector of the VRS Main Staff. It's entitled "Intelligence Report," and take a moment to look at the first page, the different matters that are being discussed here about pressures being put on the FRY by the West, activities of officers of the HVO. The bottom of the page in English: "On the 14th of May, diversionary activities of Muslims ..." And if we could please go to the middle of the second page, please, in both languages. You'll see here, General Gajic, a paragraph beginning with "The commands of the 218th Light Brigade." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It talks about how the commands of the 218th Light Brigade and the 28th Division in Srebrenica are disseminating information that our forces are planning to sever the corridor between Srebrenica and Zepa, and hence they have sent a company from the 281st Light Brigade to the area of the village of -- I'm sorry for my mispronunciation, Podravanje, and they have deployed two other companies for securing the corridor. We have confirmed reports that the command of the 28th Division is carrying out preparations for offensive operations from the Srebrenica enclave and Zepa to link up with parts of the 23rd, 26th, and 24th Divisions." Have you been following me, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page, please, in both versions. And can we please scroll down in the B/C/S version, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll see, General, that this report comes from Zdravko Tolimir, and I'd like you please to focus your attention on the very last line under "CC." You see there the very last line at the bottom of your page it says UP, GS, VJ. That P is actually a typographical error, isn't it? That should be UB for security administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So this document was sent to the security administration of the VJ General Staff and the 2nd administration of the General Staff of the VJ; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness P1831, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, this is a document. It's dated the 18th of May, 1995. It's from the intelligence and security section of the VRS Main Staff. It's titled "Intelligence Information." And we see reports on the first page about foreign affairs ministers of EU countries who were meeting in Lisbon, dissemination of information by the West.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could please turn to page 3 in both English and B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Towards the middle of the page, General Gajic, in your version, we see a paragraph that begins with the phrase "Muslim propaganda." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: According to that paragraph: "Muslim propaganda is emphasising alleged VRS operations towards enclaves in the Podrinje region. They have started occupying UNPROFOR check-points in the Srebrenica area, while in the Gorazde area, on the Gorazde-Ilovaca road, they're using UNPROFOR vehicles to manoeuvre forces and transport materiel and technical equipment, which all indicates that they are preparing offensive operations from the enclaves." So again, in this information we see information regarding the preparation of offensive operations from enclaves that are close to the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we scroll down, please, at the bottom of the B/C/S version. And can we go to the next page in English. Thank you. And further down in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What we see, General, that this document came from Petar Salapura. And we see under -- at the very bottom of the CC section we see: "UB of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army." That's the security administration, isn't it? Your former administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So again, this is an example of information sent from the VRS intelligence and security sector that was sent to your administration in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we see Exhibit P2184, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, this document is dated 19th of May, 1995, from the intelligence affairs sector of the Main Staff of the VRS. It's entitled "Intelligence Report." And on the first page we see information about Muslims who are illegally importing weapons and military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 in the English version and page 2 in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, if you could direct your attention to the first full paragraph on the page in front of you beginning with "We have confirmed ..." It says: "We have confirmed the information that the 28th Division is undergoing intensive preparations for offensive activities in order to link up with parts of the 23rd Division in the Han Pogled sector. As part of the offensive preparations from the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, they have taken possession of important facilities to secure the corridor linking the enclaves, and they have partially grouped forces in the western part of the enclaves. They have taken Podravanje, Ljeskovik, Susica, Stublic, Brloznik, Sadilov Cair, Godjenje, and Ljubomislje, and Gusinac, which are outside the so-called demilitarised zone, in order to take better conditions for offensive activities." Now, that 28th Division, that's 28th Division of the ABiH, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can we scroll down in the B/C/S version, please, and can we please go to the last page of the English version. I'm sorry, can we go back one page back in English, to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see, General, that this came from Major General Tolimir. And if we go one page further in the English, please, we see that this document was also sent to the security administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness Exhibit P2178.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This document is dated the 21st of May, 1995. It's from the intelligence and security sector of the Main Staff of the VRS. It's titled "Intelligence Report," and we see information on the first page about intelligence services of Western countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 2 in the English and page 2 in B/C/S, please. And can we focus on the top of the page in the B/C/S version. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, General, you'll see at the top of the page in your version it says: "The Muslims in the Gorazde enclave continued with the supply of ammunition by air and establishing and maintaining a high level of combat readiness. The command of the 81st Division is disseminating information that it has allegedly abandoned offensive operations due to the losses suffered by the 82nd Division at Treskavica. We have confirmed reports that in the recent period they obtained fuel," something is crossed out and then written by hand, "from UNPROFOR. The Muslim leadership is trying to avoid medical evacuation and prevent the abandonment of the enclave." Then in the next paragraph it says: "They are trying to organise the return of the population to Gorazde under the pretext of reuniting families. On the territory of Srebrenica, the Muslims are reinforcing and replenishing forces along the forward line of defence, particularly in the Suceska area." Have you been following me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, indeed I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So now we have information about another enclave that's quite close to the border of the FRY; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we scroll down in the B/C/S version, please, and in the English version. Can we go to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see this document also comes from Petar Salapura, and in the CC section, the last line, we see this document was sent to the UB, the security administration of the VJ General Staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness P2180.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, this document is dated now the 26th of May, 1995. It is from the intelligence and security sector of the Main Staff of the VRS. It's entitled "Intelligence Report."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down this page in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph from the bottom, General, we see the -- it begins with "The Muslim media." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "The Muslim media are euphorically reporting on the allegedly large number of victims among the civilian population on the territory of Tuzla, and in so doing wish to force the continuation of NATO air-strikes against VRS features and positions." Now, the fact that NATO air-strikes might occur in an area relatively close to the border of the FRY, that's something that the security administration of the VJ General Staff would have been interested in. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please go to the last page -- actually, the second to last page in English, which is one page ahead, and the next page in B/C/S, please. And if we could focus on the bottom of the page, actually, please, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, you will see that this document is from Colonel Jovica Karanovic, and in the CC section it is being sent as well to the security administration of the General Staff of the VJ. Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So there was information from the VRS security and intelligence organs forwarded to your administration during the war, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness D269. It's Exhibit D269.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, Mr. Lukic discussed this document with you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we scroll down in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see at the top of this document it begins with the title "Report number 2-107/1 on the state of the Muslim forces in the Zepa enclave." And then the next paragraph begins with: "Having taken the Srebrenica enclave, VRS units concentrated their forces around the Zepa enclave ..." And we see that this report was submitted by the 2nd administration of the VJ General Staff to General Perisic on the 14th of July, 1995. So let's just take this step-by-step. This document shows that by the 14th of July, the security administration of the VJ General Staff had information that the VRS had taken the Srebrenica enclave; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I did not hear an English translation to what the witness -- to the witness's response.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "That is correct, sir," said the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on that day, the 14th, the security administration sent that information to Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. Thank you, sir. Thank you for that correction. Prior to the 14th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm lost. You said, And on that day, the 14th, the security administration sent that information to Momcilo Perisic. The answer is, No, sir. Question, All right. The intelligence administration. What about the intelligence administration?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, I believe you were correcting a proposition in my question. I had put the question to you that it was the security administration that provided this information to General Perisic, but in your response you corrected me by saying that, No, this information came from the intelligence administration. Have we got it right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have understood me perfectly now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very important that the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And put another way, when it says the 2nd administration of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, that's a reference to the intelligence administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So prior to the 14th, do you know that -- whether the intelligence administration had received information that the VRS offensive at Srebrenica had begun? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were reports about those combat activities in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Prior to the 14th.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall, sir, what was -- what were the first reports or the first information that you received about the VRS combat activities in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, it was quite a long time ago. I can't remember all the details. If you were to show me a document, perhaps that would assist me. Now, whether it was the beginning of July or -- or a date around there, I really cannot be more precise, but I do know that there were reports roughly of this kind of content that there were operations, provocations from the Srebrenica zone, and the reaction the Army of Republika Srpska. Those reports had that kind of content.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall if those reports were coming to your administration in July of 1995 on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, perhaps not every day, but they did come on a more or less regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already answered, but I think Mr. Saxon should be more precise, on page 13, line 15, when he says "those reports," because before that he asked when he first heard about that, and then perhaps he could ask the witness on the basis of which reports he had that information. I don't think the question was precise enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the question. That's the answer. The statement "those reports had that kind of content" is the answer. I'm talking about line 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw my objection, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this information that was coming to your administration about events around Srebrenica prior to 14th of July, your administration would have also passed that information on to General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Those were reports of the intelligence administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and copies of those reports would go to General Perisic, but the 2nd administration quite regularly did send a copy of those reports to the security administration as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So thank you for that clarification. So the point being these reports about events around Srebrenica prior to the 14th of July would have been sent -- would have been passed by the intelligence administration to General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I didn't quite understand your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My mistake probably. I initially asked you a moment ago whether your administration, the security administration, would have passed on information about the events around Srebrenica prior to the 14th of July on to General Perisic, and you corrected me. And if I understood your point, your point is, it would have been the intelligence administration that would have passed this information on to General Perisic. Have I got it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but I must add to that, and I apologise. The intelligence administration, and I spoke about that yesterday, would send a copy of those reports to the operations centre of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia so that the duty team would enter it in their report for the Chief of the General Staff, the contents of those reports. I apologise for not saying that at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. All right. I'm going to move to another topic now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We can remove this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, yesterday, you and I were discussing members of the Army of Yugoslavia who went to serve in the VRS or the SVK, and at pages -- if I read our discussions at pages 71, 75, 76 of -- of the LiveNote transcript, your position appears to be that all those members of the VJ who went to serve in the VRS and/or the SVK did so voluntarily. Have I summarised your position accurately?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit P822, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, I'll give you a moment to take a look at this document. This is a court judgement. It's from the 2nd Municipal Court in Belgrade, and it refers to a legal matter brought by Dragomir Milosevic. And in the second paragraph entitled "Judgement" -- actually, if we stay with the first paragraph, we see here that the parties are Dragomir Milosevic against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro. And then if we move to the paragraph that's entitled "Judgement," it says that: "The claim brought by the plaintiff Dragomir Milosevic from Belgrade ... is hereby partly upheld, and the SRJ-SMO State is ordered to compensate the plaintiff for the nonmaterial damages he suffered and to pay the following amounts ..." And then we see a series of amounts in dinars. Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm following, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could we scroll down in the B/C/S version, please, and in the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see there's a section called "Statement of Reasons." And just briefly, the very start says: "In his claim and through his authorised agent during trial, the plaintiff alleged that on 17 May 1995, he was wounded in the course of combat activities on the Bosut facility in the general sector of Zlatiste near Sarajevo." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am following.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please turn to page 3 in both languages, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I'd like to focus on the bottom of page 3 in the English version and the top of page 3 in the B/C/S version, if we can. And, General, you'll see at the top of your version it says that: "The plaintiff Dragomir Milosevic ... stated that he had retired on the 1st of February 1997. Prior to that he had been a professional officer of the JNA army, and then the Army of Yugoslavia, that he had served in the Army of Republika Srpska in Sarajevo with the rank of major general, that from 1993 until his retirement, he has resided and worked in Sarajevo, although he was registered with military post 3001 Belgrade." Been following me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which paragraph is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In your version, General, it should be at the top of page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, we're on the wrong page on e-court. That's the problem in B/C/S. We need page 3 in e-court. We need the next page, please, and can we please focus in on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll give you just a moment, General, to read what I've just actually read out in English. Do you see that text there now, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in that paragraph it continues: "He had lived and worked for years in Sarajevo as a professional JNA officer when the war broke out and was on the records of military post 3001 Belgrade while serving in Sarajevo-Lukavica." And then it says: "Furthermore, he stated that before the establishment of the State of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, professional JNA officers who originated from Serbia were invited to state in writing whether they wanted to return to Serbia, that, since he had been born in Serbia in Murgaz, Ub municipality --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "... the plaintiff had stated in writing that he wanted to live and work in Serbia as a professional officer, which was accepted so that he was assigned to military post 3001 Belgrade. But a decision was made in the form of a written order that as a member of this military post, he would serve in Sarajevo as a member of military post 7598 Sarajevo. That is how it happened that on 17 May 1995, he was wounded during combat operations at the Bosut facility ..." Have you been following me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, this court judgement indicates that General Dragomir Milosevic did not go to serve in the VRS voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the question in the way it has been put by Mr. Saxon cannot be put in this way. Mr. Saxon has just said what Mr. Milosevic stated as a party to the proceedings, and the question has been worded differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand your objection, sir. Are you saying Mr. Saxon is embellishing what's on the record of the court?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Saxon has read shows that this is not the judgement of the court but a statement of the plaintiff, but the question put by Mr. Saxon in this way gives the impression that it is part of the court judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I can rephrase my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The version of events provided by Dragomir Milosevic and as recorded in this document indicates that Dragomir Milosevic did not go to serve in the VRS voluntarily. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of his statement, yes. That is his statement. That is what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move to a different topic now. We can move from this document. Yesterday, General, in response to a question from Mr. Lukic, you said that during the war you never received any official intelligence reports about crimes in Srebrenica or Sarajevo. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to focus, please, on the subject of crimes that occurred in Sarajevo. In your testimony yesterday, you referred to official intelligence reports. My first question for you is, during the war did you receive any official reports from VJ units outside the intelligence organs describing crimes committed by Serb forces against Muslims in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure that I heard the interpretation properly, so I would ask the interpreter to -- to repeat this question once again. Line -- page 19, line 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the interpreter please repeat this question at page 19, line 18. Are you there, interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter just repeated the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I do not recall any such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. During the war -- [B/C/S on English channel].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I just heard something in my earphones. I don't know whether it's important or not. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I also heard it. It looks like there is a crossed line on the interpretation. Even before that, since we started this morning, there is somebody in another language in the background on my earphone. I don't know whether I'm the only one who's hearing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: As you've pointed it out, Your Honour, I can vaguely hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, and it's been disturbing me the whole morning, by I thought I'll bear it, but now it's getting louder and louder. I don't know whether there's anything that can be done by the technicians to help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will proceed, and hopefully the technicians are attending to the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, during the war did you receive any official reports from other FRY institutions or agencies, that is, apart from the Army of Yugoslavia, describing crimes committed by Serb forces against Muslims in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I do not remember any such reports, either, reaching me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the war, apart from official military or government reports, then, did you receive any information at all about crimes committed by Serb forces against Muslims in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered that question, sir. I don't remember receiving any report at all about the crimes against Muslims. I don't remember. Therefore, I'm unable to say. If you have any evidence or something that you're willing to show me, perhaps then we can take it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps my question wasn't as clear as it could have been. Up to now I've been asking you questions about official reports because that was the basis of your testimony yesterday in response to a question from Mr. Lukic, and you've explained very clearly now that you've not received any official reports from the government of the former Yugoslavia, from the VJ army, about crimes committed in Sarajevo against Muslims. So let's leave the universe of official reporting. Okay. Let's leave that universe now. During the war, did you receive any information at all about crimes committed by Serb forces against Muslims in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was no official information that came our way. There were reports in the media, but those were quite contradictory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, you're saying as far as you remember, there was no official information. The question is, forget about official information; you're being asked about information from anywhere. It does not have to be official. Try to listen to the question, and try to answer the question as succinctly as you possibly can. Mr. Saxon is no longer talking about official reports now or official information. He's talking about any information. It could be from the newspaper, from the radio, from TV, from gossip, from anywhere. You can answer. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can try to be of assistance. When one says "information" in the Serbian language, it sounds official. The word -- the word "information" itself in the Serbian language sounds like an official document, and that is why I think it is a good idea that you, Your Honour, have explained to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... information cannot be a document. And I don't know B/C/S, but I can't leave that the word "information" can mean a document. I'm surprised that it actually means "official."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian language the word is often used in that sense, meaning an official report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what -- what do you say in the Serbian language if you want to talk about unofficial information?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Did you have any indication."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, we've explained the question to the witness. I think the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thank you for this intervention. I understand the question. The answer is, yes, there were reports in the media. It was from the media that we gleaned [realtime transcript read in error "cleaned"] our earliest information regarding the crimes in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, I'm asking you now to focus on information regarding crimes in Sarajevo. That's what I've been asking you about. So let's stay with Sarajevo, please. Okay? I'll ask the question this way: Did you receive any - I'm afraid to use the word now - information or indications in the media or other unofficial sources about crimes committed by Serb forces against Muslims in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we have the media reports, but we also had intelligence about the situation in Sarajevo, the siege of Sarajevo, the fighting between the Muslim armed forces and the VRS. As for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, can I ask you to please listen to the question and answer the question that is asked. Now, again you're bringing us back to official information now, because you are now saying, Sir, we have the media reports, but we also had the intelligence. Forget about intelligence, because that's official information. You're being asked about unofficial information, and please stick to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you for your intervention. There were media reports, and it could be seen on TV, things about the crimes that were shown there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you be a little bit more specific, sir. What things could be seen on television?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically the Markale incident, but there were conflicting reports, and it was difficult to understand what exactly had occurred there. That much I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Markale incident in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Prior to August of 1995, let's go back to, let's say, 1992, 1993, 1994, beginning of 1995. Did you see any reports on television -- excuse me, any indications on television indicating that crimes might be committed, were being committed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't remember that. From 1993 to April 1994, I was not in the security administration. I had a different post elsewhere, and I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, the questions I'm asking you have nothing to do with where you were working at the time. I'm asking you about what you saw on television. I'm talking about unofficial information, unofficial indications. So my question for you is: During 1992, 1993, 1994, first half of 1995, did you see indications on television that Serbian forces might be committing crimes against Muslims in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, apart from Markale, I had no other knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's turn our minds to the events in Srebrenica. General Gajic, during the war - so that would be now through Dayton, the end of 1995 - did you receive any official reports -- actually, I should back up just so we can do this as clearly as possible. In your testimony yesterday, you confirmed that you never received any official intelligence reports about crimes in Srebrenica. So my question for you now, sir, is: During the war, did you receive any official reports from VJ units or organs outside the intelligence organs describing crimes committed by Serb forces against Muslims in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, not as far as I remember, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the war did you receive any official reports from other FRY institutions or agencies apart from the VJ describing crimes committed by Serb forces against Muslims in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's go into the realm now of unofficial information or unofficial indications. During the war did you receive any unofficial information or indications about crimes committed by Serb forces against Muslims in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, again from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what information did you receive?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I remember, one of the foreign news agencies, I believe sometime around July, it's very difficult for me to pinpoint the exact point in time, spoke to one of the eyewitnesses, and then the witness described the crimes in Srebrenica and stated what he knew about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this information in the news media came to your attention at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand that question, sir. The witness has just told you what he heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Absolutely right, sir. It's Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did you do with this information when you received it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, those were individual indications, unverified at the time. Quite simply, I found it difficult when I read that, when I familiarised myself with that, to even believe it. I simply could not bring myself to believe that anything like that had happened. There was a lot of conflicting coverage and reports in the press and in the media, generally speaking. It was very difficult to wade through all that conflicting information at the time and arrive at an accurate assessment of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did you do with that conflicting coverage and reports in the media if -- did you do anything with it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, no, we didn't. This wasn't a counter-intelligence issue, if I may put it that way. This would have been the subject of an intelligence report, and that was for other bodies such as the judicial bodies, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I want to make sure I understand your evidence when you say this wasn't a counter-intelligence issue. The report -- the media report or the information that you received was that a large number of Muslims had been killed by Serb forces in around Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the media claimed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Srebrenica is close, geographically close to the border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When large numbers of people are killed, that often leads to additional humanitarian problems, like flows of refugees.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And a big part of your job was assessing information, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And wouldn't it have been relevant to the security of the state of the FRY that there might be additional humanitarian problems so close to the FRY border?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, sir. This would have constituted a humanitarian problem, but quite certainly also a security problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So how is it that you say that this was not an issue related to counter-intelligence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, only insofar as what I explained yesterday about the Muslim soldiers escaping from Zepa into Serbia's territory. Had that been the case with Srebrenica, it no doubt would have constituted a security problem, and security officials would have been there to make sure those people were adequately taken care of and put up, those fleeing the Srebrenica area. As far as the Srebrenica area itself was concerned, of course we were following the situation to make sure whether there would be waves of refugees that we would then be treating in keeping with International Law of War and all the other humanitarian laws on conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be an appropriate time, or would you like to ask that one question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour, but may I ask that one question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So -- then I'll ask you again, sir, a question I asked a few moments ago. Are you saying you did nothing with this information, as conflicting as it might have been? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, sir. I also said that it would have been other bodies that would have been in charge of reacting to something like that, primarily the judicial bodies, but also the VRS, as well as other bodies at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Shall we take the first break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I continue, there is a small error in the transcript that I'd like to ask to be changed. This is at page 23, line 10, and the witness is speaking about reports in the media, and in the transcript, English transcript, it says, "It was from the media that we cleaned our earliest information," and I think that should be "gleaned" with a G as opposed to a C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, before the break we were talking about these media reports related to the events in Srebrenica that -- that reached you in July of 1995. Can you tell us, sir, did -- did any person or part of the VJ General Staff act on these reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 26, line 4. The witness answered that information in a foreign publication was published sometime in July 1995, but he didn't say when he heard that information, and now the Prosecutor is implying as if he had heard about it in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I was actually instructed by the Bench earlier that the witness had -- had said that there were foreign news agencies, I believe sometime around July, and the witness described the crimes in Srebrenica and stated what he knew about them, and you, yourself, Your Honour, indicated to me that I didn't need to ask the witness whether that came to his attention at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, where are you reading now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Page 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Beginning at line 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What did I say? When -- when did the Bench instruct you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Line 10, Your Honour, when I asked what was, in fact, a redundant question, and you politely urged me to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. And I didn't indicate when he had heard. When he had heard, he mentions himself in the answer at line 2 -- at line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. I'll tell you what my problem is with your question, Mr. Saxon. Just give me a moment. At page 28, starting at line 6, the witness has told you what they did. He says: "As far as the Srebrenica area itself was concerned, of course we were following the situation to make sure whether there would be waves of refugees that we would then be treating in keeping with International Law of War and all the other humanitarian laws on conventions." Then you said at line 16: "So then I'll ask you again, sir, a question I asked you a few moments ago. Are you saying you did nothing with this information?" Now he's just told you what they did, you know, and your current question is still going in that line; you still want to know what they did. He has told you what they did, unless you want to say that they do anything else in addition to what he has already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I read your ruling on page 26, line 10, in relation to what I said a minute ago. Nevertheless, I stand by my previous objection. If you could please test that again. I'm trying to see what Mr. Saxon actually wanted to ask. You see at lines 4 through 7, the answer that we see there. Perhaps it's not a good idea to say this in front of the witness, but the answer doesn't show what Mr. Saxon is implying in his question. "[In English] Sir, as far as I remember, one of the foreign news agencies, I believe sometime around July. It's very difficult for me to pinpoint the exact point in time, spoke to the one of eyewitness, and then the witness described the crimes in Srebrenica and the state." [Interpretation] He talks about a conversation with this witness that was published in July, but he never actually said when he found out about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. So you want Mr. Saxon to find out when he found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why can't you do that in re-examination if he doesn't know how to find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because in this question Mr. Saxon is putting it to the witness that he heard that in July, whereas in -- in fact the witness's answer does not suggest that. I'm talking about Mr. Saxon's last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, earlier today you referred to a foreign media report sometime in July of 1995 about the events around Srebrenica. Do you recall when you saw or heard that foreign media report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I remember, and again I have to say I can't pinpoint the date, but it might have been 10 or 15 days later, before I had an opportunity to read that. I'm not sure if it was one of the printed media in the FRY that carried the report or not. I'm not certain. Nevertheless, it did occur at least 10 to 15 days later, after the foreign news agency first published the account. I'm not sure if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, 10 or 15 days later than what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, after the foreign news agency first published the account, 10 or 15 days later, a newspaper from the FRY also carried the account of this eyewitness who described the crimes in Srebrenica. I'm not sure if that makes it any clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Until we know when the foreign media carried it out, we are not able to add 10 or 15 days later. So if you tell us when the foreign media reported that news, then we can add 10 or 15 days later to -- to determine when you became aware of it. Are you able to tell us when the foreign media reported the news?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I remember, sometime after the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's as far as we can go, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we move into -- actually, one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know, General Gajic, after these reports appeared in the media in Belgrade, do you know whether particular organs in the VJ General Staff took any particular measures with respect to these reports?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, not as far as I remember. It was a different country. Republika Srpska was a different country. It had its own judiciary, its own army, and this would have been something for them to deal with. It was certainly beyond our own remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move into private session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness what is D268, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll recall, General Gajic, that Mr. Lukic discussed this document with you yesterday. It was at page 29 of the LiveNote, lines 1 through 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can we go to the next page, please, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This has to do with the role of foreign mercenaries fighting against the Serbian people. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And starting at the first line of page 29, this is what you said, you said: "So this discusses the role of Croatia in the illegal arming and making it possible for foreign mercenaries to cross its territory and use their civilian and military infrastructure in order to reach Bosnia and Herzegovina by illegal channels even before the clashes ever broke out in 1992 over in Bosnia and Herzegovina and even before Bosnia and Herzegovina became an independent country." And then you said at line 9: "So Croatia was counter-acting the resolutions of the Security Council." Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, is it your position that in March, April, early May 1992, the JNA was essentially a neutral player in the escalating conflict between the ethnic Serb and Muslim communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is Exhibit P164, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see here a cover sheet dated the 10th of December, 1991, from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. This is being sent to the commander of the 9th corps, and it says: "We hereby enclose the directive of the Federal Secretary for National Defence on the use of the armed forces in the forthcoming period."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you'll see, General Gajic, we see this is entitled the same title, the directive: "The directive on the use of the armed forces for the preparation and performance of combat operations in the forthcoming period."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go first to the last page in both versions and focus on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll see, General Gajic, this directive comes from army General Veljko Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm following.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please go to page 3 in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, I'd like you to focus on the paragraph underneath II which says the following: "Our armed forces are entering a new period of exceptional significance for accomplishing the ultimate aims of the war: protection of the Serbian population, a peaceful resolution of the Yugoslav crisis, and the creation of conditions in which Yugoslavia may be preserved for those peoples that wish to live in it." General Kadijevic did not mention the protection of the Croat population, did he?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I have an explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Kadijevic did not mention the protection of the Muslim population, did he?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I have an explanation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so by the end of 1991 - this is December now - the JNA had evolved from a multi-ethnic military force whose purpose was the protection of all peoples in Yugoslavia into a military force whose purpose it was to protect Serbian interests. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness what is Exhibit P185.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, this document dated the 20th of March, 1992, it's directed to the attention of the Chief of the General Staff. It's from the command of the 2nd Military District. That would have been the JNA's military district that would have included Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's from Commander, General Milutin Kukanjac, and on the cover page it says: "Enclosed with the document, please find the requested assessment with annexes concerning the situation and problems in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." Can you take --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please. And the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to give you a moment to review that first page. If we can, at the very top of that page under "General comments," it says: "Attached to this evaluation please find the following maps: "Deployment of the JNA volunteer units in the zone of the 2nd VO ..?" "VO" stands for "military district;" is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in both languages, please. And here I'd like to correct an error in the English translation. Can we scroll down in the B/C/S version, please. Can we go up in the B/C/S version then. If we could go forward one more page in B/C/S, please. Okay. And if we could focus on paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, you'll see towards the bottom of paragraph 3(a), we see a date there. It's about four lines up from the bottom of the paragraph, and in your version it says 3 to 4 March 1992, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, in that same paragraph where it says 3 to 4 April, that's an error; it should actually say March. And if we can please turn to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where does the correction come from? Why do you want to change this to March? How did this error come about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The error is in the English translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the witness has clarified that it's March. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's all. If we can please turn to page 6 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S version, please. Actually, can we scroll up in English, please. And can we go back one page in B/C/S. Thank you. And focus on the bottom of the page. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, you'll see there the number 5 in parentheses, and it says, "Volunteer forces in the 2nd Military District zone ..." Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: First it says: "The volunteer units in the 2nd Military District zone are indicated on the map and in the legend in great detail. In this connection, the following should also be pointed out: The listed units are organised in companies, detachments and battalions." And it says, then, in subparagraph (b): "The enlisted men number 69.198." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we briefly leave this document -- actually, no. Stay here for a moment, I think. Under (c) it says: "No volunteers are potential conscripts for the regular units of the 2nd Military District, and only a small number are from the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In other words, the volunteer units are not part of the JNA and the TO establishment structure."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I apologise. RJ is not an abbreviation for regular units but wartime units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. And are you following me with the rest of subparagraph (c)?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: These volunteer units were not part of the JNA or the TO establishment structure because these were Bosnian Serb volunteers. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir, what the actual personnel were, but I know that according to the rules in force at the time in the Yugoslav People's Army, it was lawful to form volunteer units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's keep moving here. If you take a look at subparagraph (d), it refers to numbers of men in the corps zones, and then we see in subparagraph (f): "The JNA has distributed 51.900 weapons (75 per cent), and the SDS 17.298." We're talking about distribution of weapons to Bosnian Serb volunteers, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question, sir, regarding the composition of the personnel and the rules of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Isn't your evidence, General Gajic, that the JNA at this time was distributing weapons to Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I do not have the necessary information, so I'm unable to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Subparagraph (g) says: "In Sarajevo, 300 automatic rifles have been distributed so far to retired officers (reliable ones), and in the next 3 to 4 days another 100 people will be armed ..." If we go back up the page a little bit to this number, the enlisted men number, 69.198, these enlisted men eventually became part of the Army of Republika Srpska, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know. Probably. Probably the number were included, but whether they all were, I don't know. I don't have the necessary information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Focus on this number in subparagraph (b): "The enlisted men number 69.198." Keep that number in your mind for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit P186.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a -- part of the legend to General Kadijevic's [sic] directive, and if you just take a look at the total in the column on the right, you see the -- we see the word "TOTAL" in all capital letters and then the number 69.198. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it's broken down -- if you take a look at the -- I don't -- the first seven to ten municipalities on this legend, they are all municipalities in the Sarajevo area, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. The first seven?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first seven are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But we see that there are also men available in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for example, number 52, Banja Luka, 2.000 men. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sanski Most, 1.000 men, et cetera. These are the volunteer units that were mentioned in the previous document as are indicated in the legend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see my colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether Mr. Saxon made a mistake on page 42, line 5, when he said that this document was an attachment to the directive of the General Kadijevic. I think it's an attachment to General Kukanjac's document. I think. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mr. Lukic for that correction. He's absolutely right. I misspoke. It is an attachment to P185, which was the document from General Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, these documents were produced in March of 1992, and it's true, isn't it, that prior to the outbreak of hostilities, Bosnian Serb forces, you can call them volunteer, what you will, were supported by the JNA's provision of weaponry and material to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I saw and concluded, these were volunteer units, and I told you what I had to say about volunteer units. But allow me to say something, because you didn't give me a chance to do that in answer to a couple of your questions. I said yes, but I have an explanation. You have given me quite a lot of information here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may continue. I think causes and effects have been confused here. I have been following very carefully what you have been saying, but in the reports and the assessments that you have shown, you have left out some very significant segments which refer to an assessment of the situation in the territory of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and the position that the Yugoslav People's Army found itself in, and all the measures that were taken were preventive measures, because all our assessments and indubitable evidence showed that both in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina a war was in the offing and being prepared against the JNA. We may, if you feel it necessary, to analyse these documents, looking at them from this other side, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If my colleague wants to discuss angles from the other side, he can certainly do that on re-direct examination. But you describe these measures taken by the Yugoslav People's Army as preventive measures. Within this concept of preventive measures, would that include assisting units, Bosnian Serb units, in driving out non-Serbs from communities such as Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that was not the plan or the order or the project of the JNA. Quite the contrary, in fact. There is incontrovertible evidence to the contrary. In Croatia, both Croats and Serbs who were facing threats took refuge in JNA barracks. There is, I repeat, hard incontrovertible evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, I can't show the witness something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to read some evidence that this Chamber has received, General?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, without giving the source of this evidence, it is Exhibit P80. It's a public exhibit. And I'm going to read from paragraphs 63, 65, and 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, according to one witness in this case, there was a specific chronology in this sequence of events, referring to events in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the first part of 1992. "Similar things had occurred in Bijeljina, Zvornik, and also in Visegrad."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please take this off the screen, please. I didn't ask that this -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "And also in Visegrad, although I was not familiar to which extent this had occurred in Visegrad. The volunteers would first come to a certain place and then the killings, liquidations, the intimidation of the population, panic, and so forth would follow. Then the JNA would come in with the ostensible intention of establishing order. However, all this would frighten the Muslim population, and they would be ethnically cleansed. The fact that the army arrived in Bratunac two or three days after the volunteers points to the fact that the same pattern of events would be followed in Bratunac. All these events were conceived with the goal of enabling the Serbs to take over power, and all this was connected with the implementation of plan A and plan B and the creation of Republika Srpska." From the same witness, paragraph 65: "The first part of events is related to April 1992 and the municipalities of Zvornik, Bijeljina, Bratunac, Visegrad, and Srebrenica, and must be linked to the moving out of the population. These events, in effect, led to the population moving away from the Podrinje region. I'm absolutely convinced that none of these events were accidental. All the events had been planned." And from paragraph 67: "The conduct of the JNA, which was the official army at the time, also bears out this thesis. The JNA remained in Bosnia until 15 May. It was clear that the JNA placed itself on the side of the Serbs and that it assisted in implementing the plan." Don't you agree, General Gajic, that by May 1992, the JNA was assisting Bosnian Serb forces in the ethnic cleansing of non-Serb communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I disagree. The portions of the statement that you quote contradict what Mr. Lukic was questioning me about yesterday in relation to the order of the BH Presidency, dated the 27th of April, and the order of the commander of the TO staff and interior minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 29th of April, 1992, declaring war on the JNA, after which all of the JNA barracks and installations were besieged. Therefore, according to this statement, even if the JNA had wanted to leave, it simply couldn't have left because all the roads out were blocked. Therefore, this statement is contradictory. I can understand that though. This is no more than a single person's account.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you think, sir, that the provision of arms to the SDS political party was a method to prevent violence that was used by the JNA? That's what General Kukanjac described in Exhibit P185. Was that another preventive measure to stop war from breaking out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the statement that was made that the weapons were partly distributed also to members of the SDS is possible. I would say those were military conscripts who received weapons, and politically they were in favour of the SDS. In a political sense, though, the JNA, and I don't think I should be repeating this, saw its hand forced by the Bosnian leadership, all the other institutions and the paramilitary formations involved. The JNA, and I think I can say that because I was near the very top of the hierarchy in the security administration, never meant to stir up ethnic hatred. We were and have remained a multi-ethnic army, and we loved all of the ethnic groups in the former JNA. We were brought up in that spirit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And because the JNA, as you put it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In the former Yugoslavia, not the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And because the JNA, as you put it, saw its hand forced it decided to arm Bosnian Serb units in Bosnia and Herzegovina in early 1992. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, objectively speaking, the Serbs were the ethnic group in Bosnia-Herzegovina that was in jeopardy at the time. In 1990, the Muslims had established the People's Patriotic League across Bosnia-Herzegovina, although formally they advocated a peaceful political solution to the problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In actual fact, as we saw yesterday, they opted for war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt, General. I'm going to stop you now. So then can I take your response --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's all right. Can I take your response, then, to my question as a yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can tell by looking at this that part of the weapons were distributed to Serbs, and to some extent those were volunteers units. The people described here as the SDS were people who had their wartime assignments to wartime units, but their presence was not required in the army and they were taken off this war roster. That was the normal procedure. Volunteer units were now set up, which, under the rules that applied in the JNA at the time, was allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the military leadership of the JNA approved this policy of arming the Bosnian Serb volunteer units, because, as you put it, their hand was forced.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the reaction, but the JNA was in favour of a political solution and a peaceful withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina, as was in fact later the case in the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, earlier we looked at a document that was Exhibit D268, the document about foreign mercenaries, and with respect to that document, you made the comment that Croatia was involved in illegal arming and that Croatia was counteracting the Resolutions of the Security Council. With respect to the arming of the Bosnian Serb units by the JNA, the same could be said for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time, couldn't it? It was counteracting the Resolutions of the UN Security Council?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Croatia was an internationally recognised country. Bosnian Serbs were an ethnic group within Bosnia and Herzegovina. The international recognition did not come before the 7th of April, 1992, and they were a group in jeopardy at the time. I see this as a substantial distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And, effectively, beginning in late 1991 or early 1992, the political and military leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia determined to do whatever it could to protect the Bosnian Serbs. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, can you please repeat the question. I'm not sure you were sufficiently specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the confusion stems from the period of time specified here. There is mention there of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and we know that it had not been established before May that year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I hope it's not asking too much, could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
