utterances.text: It's not asking too much. It's fine. By early 1992, it was the policy of the political and military leadership of the -- what was still then the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to do whatever was possible to protect the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the JNA and the military leadership at the time had as their main objective the preservation of the SFRY. They wanted to leave it to the politicians to decide on its future. Objectively speaking, Croatia Serbs were the group at the time facing the greatest jeopardy. Following Croatia's declaration of independence, the first law that was adopted was a set of amendments to the constitution defining the Serbs as an ethnic minority; whereas previously they had been defined as a constituent nation. Needless to say, the Serbs were not consulted on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Let me try to ask my question a bit more specifically. The -- by early 1992, the JNA was carrying out a state policy to do whatever was possible to assist and protect the Serbs in the Republika Srpska Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I would not like to repeat myself, but they were the group that was more at risk than any other group at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at the same time, the JNA was carrying out a state policy to do whatever was possible to assist and protect the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the JNA had its primary objective the task of keeping clashes from breaking out between the three ethnic groups that had up to that point in time lived side by side peacefully in a single country for 50 years. Nevertheless, political factors and a number of other influences at the time kept that from happening. What that eventually led to, regrettably, was an enormous tragedy for everyone involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I fully agree with that, General, but can I take your response to my question to be a yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that can be taken to be an affirmative answer, especially in conjunction with the explanations that I have provided previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And this state policy continued even when the SFRY became the FRY, and that state policy continued, really, throughout 1992, 1993, and until the Dayton Peace Accords at the end of 1995. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yugoslavia state and military leadership advocated a peaceful solution, and they consistently backed all the peace initiatives of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The policy I was referring to was the policy to do whatever was possible to assist the Serbian populations in Republika Srpska Krajina and the Republika Srpska. That's the policy I was referring to, sir. So my question was, the JNA and then later the VJ, continued to carry out that policy until the end of the war, until the Dayton Peace Accords in late 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just because of the significance of this particular question and answer, could we please specify what policy we are talking about. This question has been dragging on for some time, and I think the witness should be told in no uncertain terms which period of time is in question and in what way the SFRY Presidency gave its backing to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think the witness, first of all, has answered my question with respect to the first part of 1992. The policy, I stated very clearly in my question, it's at line 25 of page 50, onto line 1 of page 51, but I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, with respect to this state policy to try and assist and protect the Serbian communities in the Republika Srpska and the Republika Srpska Krajina, that remained state policy of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia through the end of the war in 1995, through the Dayton Peace Accords, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the JNA, and then later the VJ, continued then to carry out that state policy through the end of the war; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think I have answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But I need -- well, just so the record's clear, is the answer "Yes"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the VJ's efforts to carry out this state policy to protect, Serb populations in Republika Srpska Krajina and the Republika Srpska, that included, for example, the deploying -- or transferring of officers from the VJ to the armies of the Republika Srpska and the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think I explained that yesterday, but I'll repeat anyway. There were several different categories of officers in the VRS. As far as the VJ is concerned, it was on a voluntary basis that officers were seconded to the VRS, specifically those who had been born in Republika Srpska and were serving in the VJ. The same applied to any other members of the VJ who of their own free will chose to go to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Pause there, please. But it was the -- it was the policy -- became the policy and the programme of the VJ to facilitate and permit these secondments of officers; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That was a decision taken by the Supreme Defence Council and all the other supreme state bodies, including the FRY parliament. General Staff of the VJ was the body that executed all these decisions and orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. So it was the General Staff of the VJ that executed these policies.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. And the state policy to protect and assist the -- actually, let me step back for a moment. The VJ's efforts to carry out this state policy to protect Serb populations in the Republika Srpska Krajina and the Republika Srpska also included, for example, the sending of large quantities of materiel, weapons, ammunition, fuel, medical supplies to the Army of Republika Srpska and the army of the Serbian Republic of Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you mean military aid, the answer is yes. Again, pursuant to decisions taken by the appropriate state bodies, the supreme state bodies. We never tried to conceal that. It was a matter of public record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it would have been extremely difficult for the VRS and the SVK to conduct their own activities during the war without these different kinds of assistance received from the VJ. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. This is asking the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This witness is a career military officer, Your Honour, who was there at the time, and he should be able to at least provide his belief or opinion on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is he giving evidence as a military expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: He is not giving his evidence as a military expert, Your Honour, but he is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're asking for his personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is a security officer, and now his opinion is being elicited on materiel aid and its possible significance to the VRS and the SVK, two altogether different armies. I think what this leads to is pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon says he's not asking him as an expert, so he's not asking him as a security officer in the VJ but just his opinion as a military officer, and of course he's quite free to say he's able to answer the question or not able to answer that question. So your objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Shall I repeat my question, General Gajic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It would have been extremely difficult for the VRS and the SVK to conduct their own activities during the war without these different kinds of assistance received from the Army of Yugoslavia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I disagree. I believe the VRS had sufficient material resources available to it to engage in all their activities. There is another thing. I'm not sure how much you know about Serbs. Serbs tend to be able to find their way around and get places. Had it not been for the aid, they would have found another way to do what they were trying to do. Therefore, I don't think that was essential to their activity, at least not as enshrined in your original question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But because of the aid that came from the VJ, there was no need to, as you put it, find another way to do what they were trying to do; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already answered the question, on page 54, line 18 and 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think I'm asking a different question, Your Honour, based on the response of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After that answer at page 54 the witness said something else that prompted the question you asked. He said they would have other ways of finding aid elsewhere. So that's a follow-up on that answer. Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Gajic, because of the aid that came from the VJ, there was no need to, as you put it, for the VRS and the SVK to find another way to do what they were trying to do. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have different information, and that is that the Army of Republika Srpska supplied itself from other channels, from Bulgaria, Romania, for instance. They had their own channels and connections through which they supplied themselves with materiel and equipment. Even from Greece.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The senior officer corps of the VRS and the SVK were made up predominantly of officers from the Army of Yugoslavia who were seconded to the VRS and the SVK. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that's not quite correct. When the former Yugoslav People's Army ceased to exist, the largest number of senior staff born in Croatia and who had served in Croatia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina and had served in Bosnia-Herzegovina voluntarily stayed behind in the Army of the Republika Srpska and the army of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It would, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, I'd like to go back for a moment to a discussion we had before the break, and I had asked you about the VJ's efforts to carry out -- this is at page 53, beginning at line 5, and I'd asked you about the VJ's provision of military aid to the armies of Republika Srpska and the army of Serbian Republic of Krajina, and you said to me: "Sir, if you mean military aid, the answer is yes. Again, pursuant to decisions taken by the appropriate state bodies, the supreme state bodies, we never tried to conceal that. It was a matter of public record." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that the -- the VJ gave its assistance and military aid to the VRS and the SVK publicly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, when I said that it was common knowledge that the public was aware of it, there were articles in the press about it, and as far as I can remember I think this was discussed by the delegates in parliament, so it was in that context that I had in mind when I said it was in the public record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say, "We never tried to conceal that," who is the "we" that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for this question. I wasn't specific enough. I mean the state, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you include within that state, within that "we," the Army of Yugoslavia, that nor did the Army of Yugoslavia try to conceal this military aid?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Army of Yugoslavia, I don't think in public, but the state bodies presented it, but I think it was well known even to military and political representatives accredited to Belgrade. They knew about that. They were aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you're aware, aren't you, that in May 1992 the United Nations imposed sanctions against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall why those sanctions were imposed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I think the sanctions were imposed to force all the parties to deal with problems by political means in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But specifically, the sanctions were imposed against the FRY because of the FRY's assistance, military assistance, to the Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbian Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think that was the only reason. At the time, it was felt that -- or, rather, the international community felt that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not cooperative enough in those efforts to find a political settlement to the problems in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say "it was not the only reason," but the military assistance was one reason, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And these sanctions that were imposed by the UN against the FRY, they were not fully lifted until after the Dayton Accords. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they were lifted selectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: They were not fully lifted until after the Dayton Accords; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes. That's -- they were not lifted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, if sanctions are imposed on a state by the international community, such sanctions would effectively be a threat to the well-being of that state. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so it would at that time, between 1992 and the Dayton Accords, the end of 1995, it was not in the interests of the FRY to see sanctions tightened, was it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It would not, then, have been in the interests of the FRY, or of the VJ for that matter, to permit its military assistance to the RS and the RSK to occur publicly. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a bit -- I think I've answered at that question. It seems to me rather a dual question. I think I answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let me ask the question in another way. Since it was not in the interests of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to see sanctions tightened, it would have been against the interests of the FRY -- I'm going to ask the question hopefully in a simpler way. Since it was not in the interests of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to see sanctions tightened, it would have been in the interests of the FRY, and therefore of the VJ, to conceal the continued provision of military aid to the Army of Republika Srpska and the army of the Serbian Republic of Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, decisions about that aid were made by the highest state leadership, and they regulated how this aid should be extended, in what way, whether this should be known or not, et cetera. These were political decisions, the details of which I am not familiar with. They were political decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Right. Moving on to another topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, yesterday you indicated you might take a session. You have taken two. How much longer are you going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Hopefully about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit D273, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see, General, this is a report that Mr. Lukic showed you yesterday on the living conditions and presence of members of Muslim armed forces at the holding centres at Mitrovo Polje and Branesko Polje. Do you remember looking at this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says in the beginning, the first paragraph, in the period from 31 July to 25 October 1995, larger and smaller groups of Muslim armed forces entered the FRY from the Zepa area, numbering a total of 799 persons. And then these 799 persons were -- remained within these holding centres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, first of all it was the army that took them in and a commission that was formed as I described yesterday, and they were registered and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All I need is a yes or no answer to my question, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At first, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, eventually these 799 persons found their way to these holding centres; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get the interpretation. That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. This document deals with Muslims who crossed over in the period 31 July through 25 October. Do you know what happened to the Muslims who crossed the Drina River from the Srebrenica-Zepa areas and entered the FRY between the middle of July and 31 July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I know, yesterday when I was looking through those lists, I noted that among the members of the armed forces, the Muslim armed forces, there were members of the 28th Division and certain brigades from the 28th Division. And as for the period you have specified, I don't know -- or, rather, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, the truth is, General, that those Muslims who crossed over before the 31st of July were returned to the Republika Srpska and killed. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that is something that I absolutely am not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During your direct examination, this is at page 44 of the LiveNote, discussing this same document, Mr. Lukic asked you what became of these persons, the persons who are -- the 799 persons mentioned in this report. And at page 44, beginning at line 16, you said the following: "Mr. Lukic, I know that those persons were allowed to decide for themselves as to what their next destination would be upon leaving the reception centres. As far as I know, most of them headed west, most of them through Hungary. Every security measure available was taken in the process." Do you know, sir, if any of those Muslims expressed a desire to return to Republika Srpska in the last part of 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, thank you very much for your time and your patience with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll pass the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Saxon, for this co-ordination of efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, good afternoon once again.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume you wish to return to your family as soon as possible, so I shall try and focus on the most important points so that we can really finished today. My first question -- for my first question, could we go into private session, and could we put P215 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, Mr. Saxon asking you whether you stand by your thesis that these were three separate armies, showed you a set of documents that I should like us to go back to, and they relate to the personnel status of certain officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have on the screen P2128, page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll first look at the name of Mr. Tolimir. This was shown to you by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bottom part of the page when we see the data for Mr. Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief, it was stated that Mr. Tolimir, Zdravko, was assistant for -- of the Chief of Staff for intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us look at the B/C/S page 3, please. The English is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you're not very familiar with personnel affairs, but what I'm going to ask you is more in your professional field. The date mentioned is the 10th of November, 1993. You see the date, and Mr. Saxon mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it is stated, as Mr. Saxon said, that he's being appointed to the Chief of Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia in the 30th centre of the Main Staff under that date as assistant chief. Then a bit lower it says that until then, according to the peacetime establishment, he was chief of the security organ in the command of the 2nd Military District, FC Colonel PG11 as of the 30th of August, 1990, Sarajevo Garrison. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday and today we saw several documents where the 2nd Military District is mentioned and signed by General Kukanjac. Did the 2nd Military District exist until the 10th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did the 2nd Military District cease to exist?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, as far as I can remember around the 15th of May when the pull-out started, that is May 1992 when the pull out of the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina started.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the structure of the Yugoslav People's Army -- or, rather, the Army of Yugoslavia, after the formation of the Army of Yugoslavia, did the 2nd Military District exist after May 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now put on the screen document from the 65 ter list of the Prosecution, 7386. In the B/C/S page 41. This document in the set of Defence documents. Unfortunately, we do not have an English translation of this document, so I will cover it with the help of the witness, or at least parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it aloud, and could the witness just confirm whether I'm reading correctly. It is a decree by the president of the Republika Srpska, dated the 16th of December, 1992. "Pursuant to Article 11, 168 and 369 of the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska, according to peacetime and wartime establishment we appoint Tolimir Zdravko." I leave out the data, and then says in capitals: "To the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Sector for Intelligence, Security Affairs." Then I leave out again some details, and lower down it says: "Up until now, according to peacetime establishment, he was head of the administration for security, intelligence affairs in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, establishment rank major general, group 9, dated the 10th of June, 1992." Then again I leave out some of the text, we'll just see who is the signatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Signature, the President of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. Have I read out correctly this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, you read it out correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does this document tell you? In which army and when and at what position was Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this document clearly shows that Zdravko Tolimir, by decree of the president of the Republic of Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, was appointed to a general's position on the 10th of June, 1992, and to the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina, and that is the competence of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think you made a slip of the tongue. You didn't mean the Army of Krajina but the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't object to the admission of the document, but since we do not have an English translation, I'd ask that it be marked for identification at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's only fair, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's something else that I might add, and I see the Registrar was going to react. This document under number 1796P is in the evidence in the B/C/S version, but other portions have been admitted in English. If you remember, those are personnel files, and to the best of my understanding of your instructions, only what has been translated into English is part of the P evidence, and now we need to have a new number for the rest of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think we should follow the practice that we have been following all the time. Documents which belong must stay together. We'll make it part of P1796, but this part will be MFI'd until the translation is provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May we now please go back in relation to Petar Salapura, OTP Exhibit P2128, page 3 in the B/C/S, I believe. The same page number in English. You testified in relation to Petar Salapura, that he was in the intelligence organ, intelligence security organ of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can Mr. Lukic please speak closer into the microphone. The interpreter can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you heard that? Please speak closer to the microphone. The interpreter don't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we might as well keep this, this portion in English, although the name Petar Salapura occurs in the previous page. And the Prosecutor showed you this. Mr. Saxon used this document to put it to you that Petar Salapura on the 10th of November, 1993, was appointed to the 30th Personnel Centre, the General Staff of the VJ, chief of the intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first sentence that you can see in English, Your Honours, is the sentence that I will be asking the witness a question about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just as I asked you in relation to Mr. Tolimir a minute ago, I will ask you about Mr. Salapura too. Do you know that on the 10th of November, 1993, there was something called the 2nd Military District in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt. It's just -- could we have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The correct page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The correct page on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I heard Mr. Lukic earlier say, "Let's stay with this page" -- [overlapping speakers]... the previous page, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We might as well show the previous page just to make sure it's in reference to Mr. Salapura. This part of the document is in English, and that's what I am discussing with the witness. Therefore -- so just to repeat this, in English you can see number 3, first name, last name, date, the 10th of November, 1993. And what Mr. Saxon showed you yesterday. And now could we please move on to the next page and focus on my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where was he based on this document, or where had he been up to this date, I asked you. And you answered the question, Mr. Gajic. You said that on the 10th of November, 1993, there was no such thing as a 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not in the VJ at any rate. And what about February 1992? Was there such a thing as the 2nd Military District back in February?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was at that time, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm done with this document, and I'm moving on to another document that you were shown by Mr. Saxon yesterday. This requires private session. This is P2518.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we please move into private session. 16 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're -- we're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I made an objection about the transcript, about the translation specifically. I would like to read this back and the general can please confirm whether my reading is accurate. The handwritten portion, General. "Call and send if he wants. If not, a proposal." Is my reading correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, your reading is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see the discrepancy, Your Honours, between the translation. Since this is actually significant, I move that we request an official translation of the handwritten portion from CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with this person's handwriting by any chance?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, certainly. This is Momcilo Perisic, chief of the General Staff, and it actually reads "MP," Momcilo Perisic, his very own initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You just ask that we get an official translation of this document. So to be able to do that, then we must change the status of the document from an exhibit to an exhibit marked for identification pending that translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Saxon agrees, if the Chamber agrees, based on what we have just quoted in the courtroom, which was interpreted accurately, I believe, I think there is no longer a need for an official translation of the entire document. That need has been obviated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you say so. And if Mr. Saxon agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the better procedure would be to get an official translation. That's what I would ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the parties can't agree, then may we get an official translation, and for that reason, therefore, P2518 shall be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we please go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 2 -- P2103.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another document you were shown by Mr. Saxon. It's about Mr. Svetozar Kosoric. This is an order by the commander of the Drina Corps, signed by Commander General Krstic. Let me ask you, first of all, the Drina Corps was part of which army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A brief follow-up question on this document. He was appointed as a delegate of the chief of the intelligence department in the organ for intelligence security-related issues in a corps of the land forces in the 30th Personnel Centre. You were a security officer yourself. Therefore, I will ask you this: Are you familiar with the fact that within the establishment of the VJ at the time there was a post like this such as I have just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic. There was the security department of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have P1151 brought up on our screens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another document that you were shown by Mr. Saxon. You remember this document, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I do, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document by the recruitment, mobilisation sector of the General Staff of the VJ. It was sent to the personnel administration on of the 40th Personnel Centre. The last paragraph, and that's in relation to the preceding two paragraphs: "Please issue the above-mentioned person with an authorisation to return to his original unit and a receipt for the time he spent in the 40th Personnel Centre." Had the VRS been a component of the VJ, would there have to be a need for approval to be granted like this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It would have been much simpler. An order would have to be issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have P7314, B/C/S page 10, English page 7. These are instructions governing the work of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 7314 we don't have, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 734.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Instructions governing the work of the special personnel centres, dated November 1993. This is page 1, and can we please have page 10 of the English -- rather, page 10 of the B/C/S, and page 10 of the English which happens to be the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't believe you've seen this document before, General. Nevertheless, I will read out a portion to you and ask to have your position on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 33, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "In keeping with the service requirements, professional soldiers and civilian personnel sent or transferred to the personnel centre may be returned, assigned, or transferred to VJ units, institutions with the consent or on the recommendation of the KC Main Staff. Consent or recommendations for persons described under paragraph 1 herein shall be sent to the KC personnel department, which shall immediately draw up the documents stipulated and direct the persons to report to his previous unit, institution, or transfer, assign, or appoint them to a post within the purview of the VJ and GS, Chief of the General Staff and President of the FRY in the Yugoslav Army." Is this consistent with what you were shown a minute ago? Is this the kind of approval that is sought for someone to go back?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about this, sir: If someone leaves the VRS without seeking proper authorisation from the VRS, what would their status be in that army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, they would have the status of a deserter because that person is within their chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: P2598, please. The B/C/S reference is page 8, and the English is page 9. 2598. Yes, that's right. We are looking for Tihomir Babic. You remember being asked questions about him yesterday.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon talked to you about some information regarding Mr. Tihomir Babic in this document, his actual return to the VJ. The Loznica Garrison would be in the VJ; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise if the question was leading. I'm just trying to save time and conclude as soon as possible. Could this person have returned to the Loznica Garrison, could this order have been issued without previous authorisation from the Main Staff of the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic, that would not have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see Prosecution Exhibit P1856. [In English] P1856.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is another document that you were shown by Mr. Saxon yesterday, and it was about the same person?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Document of the Main Staff of the VRS sent to the command of the Drina Corps. I just want to know your position, sir, on the substance of this order. It says Tihomir Babic infantry is transferred from the 30th Personnel Centre to a VJ unit pursuant to an order by the relevant officer. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on what it says, the 30th Personnel Centre would be in the VJ, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was subordinated to the personnel administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document says -- can you take a look at what it says? He was transferred from the 30th personnel centre to a VJ unit. Does this decision effectively take him back to a VJ unit?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what it does. He's hereby returning to a VJ unit. I'm sorry, I didn't quite fully understand your question the first time around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That was quite a leading question, but I see that the witness has answered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are aware of time constraints, but we must stay within the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm done with this set of documents, and I'm about to embark on a set of questions in relation to a much-debated subject, specifically we talked about this yesterday. Were these three different armies, or in fact a single army? We have looked at a number of documents. We analysed the rules of service of the security organ suggesting that the security administration was the supreme technical body in terms of security in the VJ.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite right, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What security organ is directly subordinated to the security administration in terms of security-related issues?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that would have been the security department of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't think this question arises out of cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please be allowed to ask two further questions to explain why this is pertinent as to whether these were three different armies or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Lukic, there is an objection. You've got to deal with the objection before you can ask any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon asked a whole set of questions about whether these were in fact three different armies or not. I'm asking this question to see about the security chain of command of the VJ. I'm trying to ask the witness about the chain of command in which the VRS and SVK security organs were. I think this question stems directly from the cross-examination by Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're shaking your head, Mr. Saxon. Are you saying you never asked any question about whether these are three separate armies or one army?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, looking at the security chain of command, who was subordinated to the army security organs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it was the corps's security bodies that were subordinated to them in the security chain of command. I'm talking about the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In a technical sense, and we looked at all those documents about technical guidance, you, when I say you, I mean the security administration, were you in a position to issue any instructions or orders in terms of technical guidance to those subordinated organs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the case, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, Mr. Lukic. I don't know whether everybody else is hearing what I'm hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is phone ringing in the English booth, but we have absolutely nothing to do with that, and don't know why that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Interpreter. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You as the security administration, were you in a position to issue an order like that to any security organ from the VRS or indeed the SVK?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, a categorical answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's try to be more specific. Do you know of anyone from the security administration adopting an order, a set of instructions perhaps, an assignment for Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Beara, Mr. Raseta, or any of the security officials of those armies?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown a set of documents by Mr. Saxon today, intelligence information of the intelligence security organ of the VRS, dated May 1995. Among other addressees, there were two in the VJ, one being the personnel administration -- the security administration; the other being the intelligence administration. I would like you to focus your attention on certain types of information, primarily in relation to the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Lukic please speak closer to the microphone or speak up because I can't hear him properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters would like you to speak closer to microphone or speak up because they are not able to hear you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These reports describe the activities of which army primarily?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the activities of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about these intelligence reports? When they describe the activities of the VRS, do they focus on such information showing what the enemy was doing or what the VRS was doing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These focus on enemy activity and any reaction by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why are these reports signed by intelligence officers with the intelligence and security department of the VRS? Why not by Beara himself? Can you comment, sir, please, because we saw that all these documents were signed by intelligence officers.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the simple reason was that this was intelligence they were dealing with gathered by intelligence officers using their own methods and means. This wasn't pure counter-intelligence work, as I believe I explained to Mr. Saxon in roughly the same terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown the Dragomir Milosevic sentence from the Dragomir Milosevic trial. You saw the basis for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dragomir Milosevic sentence from his trial, or the judgement in his claim in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is P822.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Lukic please face the microphone and not away from the microphone. We really can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please face the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can't get you a longer microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You looked at the sentence. Mr. Saxon showed you the sentence. In what capacity was Mr. Milosevic heard there? I know you're not lawyer yourself.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, he was the plaintiff. He brought charges against the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the document that we were looking at, P164. We looked at that with Mr. Saxon a while ago. That is the report by General Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon showed you this document while explaining his theory that the army was not neutral, rather that it was primarily protecting the Serb interests. You answered questions about that a while ago, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Switch off the other mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave the wrong number. P5 -- [In English] P185, B/C/S 5, English 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say the number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: P185. Page 5 English, page 5 B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading what it says under (b). Mr. Saxon told you it refers to an event that occurred in March 1992 in Sarajevo. Mr. Kukanjac says here: "Thanks to a strong anti-army campaign by the SDA leadership, the mass media, and some other institutions, the majority of the Muslim population has a fairly reserved attitude towards our army. However, the role of the JNA on the said night has helped considerably to restore the confidence of the Muslim population in the JNA. The district command received the most telegrams, letters, and telephone calls from Muslims thanking us for having prevented bloodshed. We have information that the SDA and some other party leaderships are considering a plan to again turn the Muslim people against the JNA. So far they have not been successful in that." General, before the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was formed in May 1992, or, rather, during the existence the former SFRY, what was the constitutional role of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the main constitutional role of the JNA was to protect the integrity and sovereignty of the then Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In performing this task, was the JNA for or against all those who wished to remain within the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, from the very beginning the military leadership was in favour of the survival of Yugoslavia, but for the peoples of Yugoslavia to decide their own destiny and that the JNA would accept any political decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the JNA armed in those days those who wanted to leave the SFRY, that is, those with secessionist intentions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In view of this basic or fundamental constitutional role of the JNA, did it act in accordance with the decisions of the highest political leadership of the then SFRY with respect to the arming of those who recognised the SFRY and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any distinctions made on an ethnic basis of those who accepted the JNA and the constitutional order of the SFRY and were not Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there was no distinction. For as long as the JNA existed, it was absolutely multi-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether through the bodies of Territorial Defence which accepted the SFRY using those TO organs were Muslim and Croats that accepted the TO also armed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have just one more question. Let me see your answer on page 51, line 24, in answer to a question by Mr. Saxon. Here is the question put to you by Mr. Saxon: "[In English] General, with respect to this state policy to try to assist and to protect the Serbian communities in Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina, that remained the state policy of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia through the end of the war in 1995 to the Dayton Peace Accords, didn't it?" [Interpretation] Your answer was, Yes. You remember this question?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that was a sequence of questions, because according to Mr. Saxon's case, the leadership now of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Army of Yugoslavia supported the demands of Republika Srpska and the Serbian people in Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. My question is, have you heard of the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the proposal behind what plan, do you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the plan proposed that a peaceful settlement be accepted in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that the war be ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Army of Yugoslavia in respect to at that plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Army of Yugoslavia unequivocally accepted that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the position of Republika Srpska and the Army of Republika Srpska in connection with that plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the leadership of Republika Srpska and the military leadership of Republika Srpska rejected the plan, and the plan was rejected at a meeting of the Assembly of Republika Srpska. And also present on that occasion was Mr. Mitsotakis, who was at the time prime minister of Greece, and Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what was the position of President Slobodan Milosevic and Mr. Mitsotakis at that Assembly meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it was unpleasant. Every attempt to persuade the people that there was no other alternative, that the alternative was war or peace and -- however, they did not accept. Republika Srpska, the Assembly of Republika Srpska, did not accept it, and the highest leadership of that republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who proposed peace, and who proposed that the plan be accepted in that Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Milosevic on behalf of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Mitsotakis from Greece.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, have you heard of the Contact Group Plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of it. This was from August -- or, rather, from the middle of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Army of Yugoslavia with respect to that plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it was absolutely accepted by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Army of Yugoslavia as -- I would say as the last chance for achieving peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the political leadership of Republika Srpska and the Army of Republika Srpska in respect to the adoption of the Contact Group Plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, they emphatically rejected that plan, and they treated this as a betrayal of their interests, the interests of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this have certain consequences in relations between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after this, sanctions were enforced against Republika Srpska by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In view of what I read out a moment ago and that Mr. Saxon asked you about, do you still consider that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Army of Yugoslavia always supported the positions of Republika Srpska and the Army of Republika Srpska until the end of the war in 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not precise in answering that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to all of you and the interpreters for the speed of my questions, but I wanted to complete this testimony by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gajic, I have a question to put to you. To be quite honest, I have some difficulty in believing regarding what you said about the events in Srebrenica and when you said that you learnt about what was happening after the beginning of the month of August, several days after the event. I wonder, you were head of military security. Where do you get information that allows you to do your work in the field of security. Where does your information come from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, pursuant to the information we received, they came from the military intelligence administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and the intelligence information that we received from the intelligence sector of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, that information came from the ground, came from military men who were in the field.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, in spite of the fact that you had information coming directly from soldiers who were in Srebrenica during the events of the month of July, so no information reached you before the beginning of the month of August or mid-August? And again through the media, according to what you told us. It was only from the media that you learnt what had happened.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the information that I referred to, there was no information about crimes committed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I'm so astonished. You had no information of crimes committed in Srebrenica; whereas you had men on the ground who were informing you. So I really don't know. Maybe your intelligence services were not too effective, but I am having difficulty in understanding that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, those were not our intelligence organs in Republika Srpska. They were members of the intelligence organs of the Army of Republika Srpska. So that means of quite a different army, and they informed us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, but I am talking about the Yugoslav Army. You had your own men who were informing you from Republika Srpska. You did not depend exclusively on the information from the VRS.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, those operative positions, as we called them, with the collapse or break-up of Yugoslavia, most of them went abroad. So we had far more information reaching us as to what was happening abroad regarding illegal arming, mercenaries, and so on, which they sent us on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gajic, it's not credible what you're saying. Half of the officers who were in the VRS, they came from the VJ, a large number in any event, a certain percentage anyway. They were paid by you, and they were not informing you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we in the counter-intelligence had our own sources that were registered sources. They were not all members of -- not all members of the army were obliged to inform the counter-intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I won't insist, because you're not going to answer my question. I do not find you to be very credible in your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: General, I will ask you a very brief question due to the hour. The Prosecutor, as well as Mr. Lukic, showed you an exhibit in which General Dragomir Milosevic demanded the state of Serbia and Montenegro for injuries suffered during his tenure of the Republika Srpska, as he said in the narrative. My question to you: As a general of the Yugoslav Army who also had experience in the Army of Republika Srpska, as you said, why this demand even though you are not a lawyer, was not issued against Republika Srpska and only to the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro? Do you know why? Is any information in your possession, official or nonofficial, not only as a security officer but as a general and soldier of the -- of both armies.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I saw this document for the first time, and I'm really not familiar with the case, so I can't give you a proper answer and meet your interest. I'm afraid that if I were to say anything due to lack of knowledge, I could be misleading, so I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Do you know of any officer of the 30th Personnel Centre who, suffering injuries at the front in the Republika Srpska Army, had ever issued a demand against the Republika Srpska? Do you know of any case?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not. I am not familiar with any single case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are the parties going to have questions arising from the questions from the Bench? Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Gajic, that brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming to testify at the Tribunal. You are now excused. You may stand down, and please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your fairness, and I wish you a pleasant weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The matter stands adjourned to Monday, the 15th of March, at 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 15th day of March, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 25
